entries.7f8c927a30266eea320b2aa47ed2b87ad040328a: <div sID="gen13226" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="145" osisID="Ps.145" sID="Ps.145"/> <div eID="gen13226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13227" type="x-p"/> The five foregoing psalms were all of a piece, all full of prayers; this, and the five that follow it to the end of the book, are all of a piece too, all full of praises; and though only this is entitled David's psalm yet we have no reason to think but that they were all his as well as all the foregoing prayers. And it is observable, 1. That after five psalms of prayer follow six psalms of praise; for those that are much in prayer shall not want matter for praise, and those that have sped in prayer must abound in praise. Our thanksgivings for mercy, when we have received it, should even exceed our supplications for it when we were in pursuit of it. David, in the last of his begging psalms, had promised to praise God (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.9">Ps. cxlv. 9</reference>), and here he performs his promise. 2. That the book of Psalms concludes with psalms of praise, all praise, for praise, is the conclusion of the whole matter; it is that in which all the psalms centre. And it intimates that God's people, towards the end of their life, should abound much in praise, and the rather because, at the end of their life, they hope to remove to the world of everlasting praise, and the nearer they come to heaven the more they should accustom themselves to the work of heaven. This is one of those psalms which are composed alphabetically (as <reference osisRef="Ps.25">Ps. 25</reference> and 34, &c.), that it might be the more easily committed to memory, and kept in mind. The Jewish writers justly extol this psalm as a star of the first magnitude in this bright constellation; and some of them have an extravagant saying concerning it, not much unlike some of the popish superstitions, That whosoever will sing this psalm constantly three times a day shall certainly be happy in the world to come. In this psalm, I. David engages himself and others to praise God, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.1-Ps.145.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.4-Ps.145.7">4-7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.10-Ps.145.12">10-12</reference>. II. He fastens upon those things that are proper matter for praise, God's greatness (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.3">ver . 3</reference>), his goodness (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.8-Ps.145.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>), the proofs of both in the administration of his kingdom (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.13">ver. 13</reference>), the kingdom of providence (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.14-Ps.145.16">ver. 14-16</reference>), the kingdom of grace (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.17-Ps.145.20">ver. 17-20</reference>), and then he concludes with a resolution to continue praising God (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.21">ver. 21</reference>) with which resolution our hearts must be filled, and in which they must be fixed, in singing this psalm.
entries.a51afe16333f86b87d8b63e2fe90de49e37c8d28: <div eID="gen13227" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Grateful Acknowledgments.</title> <div sID="gen13228" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I will extol thee, my God, O king; and I will bless thy name for ever and ever. <hi type="super">2</hi> Every day will I bless thee; and I will praise thy name for ever and ever. <hi type="super">3</hi> Great <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and greatly to be praised; and his greatness <hi type="italic">is</hi> unsearchable. <hi type="super">4</hi> One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts. <hi type="super">5</hi> I will speak of the glorious honour of thy majesty, and of thy wondrous works. <hi type="super">6</hi> And <hi type="italic">men</hi> shall speak of the might of thy terrible acts: and I will declare thy greatness. <hi type="super">7</hi> They shall abundantly utter the memory of thy great goodness, and shall sing of thy righteousness. <hi type="super">8</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> gracious, and full of compassion; slow to anger, and of great mercy. <hi type="super">9</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> good to all: and his tender mercies <hi type="italic">are</hi> over all his works. <div eID="gen13228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13229" type="x-p"/> The entitling of this <hi type="italic">David's psalm of praise</hi> may intimate not only that he was the penman of it, but that he took a particular pleasure in it and sung it often; it was his companion wherever he went. In this former part of the psalm God's glorious attributes are praised, as, in the latter part of the psalm, his kingdom and the administration of it. Observe, <div eID="gen13229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13230" type="x-p"/> I. Who shall be employed in giving glory to God. <div eID="gen13230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13231" type="x-p"/> 1. Whatever others do, the psalmist will himself be much in praising God. To this good work he here excites himself, engages himself, and has his heart much enlarged in it. What he does, that he will do, having more and more satisfaction in it. It was his duty; it was his delight. Observe, (1.) How he expresses the work itself: "<hi type="italic">I will extol thee, and bless thy name</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.1">v. 1</reference>); I will speak well of thee, as thou hast made thyself known, and will therein express my own high thoughts of thee and endeavour to raise the like in others." When we speak honourably of God, this is graciously interpreted and accepted as an extolling of him. Again (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will bless thee, I will praise thy name;</hi> the repetition intimates the fervency of his affection to this work, the fixedness of his purpose to abound in it, and the frequency of his performances therein. Again (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will speak of thy honour,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.6">v. 6</reference>) <hi type="italic">I will declare thy greatness.</hi> He would give glory to God, not only in his solemn devotions, but in his common conversation. If the heart be full of God, out of the abundance of that the mouth will speak with reverence, to his praise, upon all occasions. What subject of discourse can we find more noble, more copious, more pleasant, useful, and unexceptionable, than the glory of God? (2.) How he expresses his resolution to persevere in it. [1.] He will be constant to this work: <hi type="italic">Every day will I bless thee.</hi> Praising God must be our daily work. No day must pass, though ever so busy a day, though ever so sorrowful a day, without praising God. We ought to reckon it the most needful of our daily employments, and the most delightful of our daily comforts. God is every day blessing us, doing well for us; there is therefore reason that we should be every day blessing him, speaking well of him. [2.] He will continue in it: <hi type="italic">I will bless</hi> thee <hi type="italic">for ever and ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.145.1-Ps.145.2">v. 1 and again v. 2</reference>. This intimates, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he resolved to continue in this work to the end of his life, throughout <hi type="italic">his ever</hi> in this world. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That the psalms he penned should be made use of in praising God by the church to the end of time, <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.30">2 Chron. xxix. 30</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That he hoped to be praising God to all eternity in the other world. Those that make praise their constant work on earth shall have it their everlasting bliss in heaven. <div eID="gen13231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13232" type="x-p"/> 2. He doubts not but others also would be forward to this work. (1.) "They shall concur in it now; they shall join with me in it: When <hi type="italic">I declare thy greatness men shall speak of</hi> it (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.6">v. 6</reference>); <hi type="italic">they shall abundantly utter it</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.7">v. 7</reference>), or <hi type="italic">pour it out</hi> (as the word is); they shall praise God with a gracious fluency, better than the most curious oratory. David's zeal would provoke many, and it has done so. (2.) "They shall keep it up when I am gone, in an uninterrupted succession (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">One generation shall praise thy works to another.</hi>" The generation that is going off shall tell them to that which is rising up, shall tell what they have seen in their days and what they have heard from their fathers; they <hi type="italic">shall</hi> fully and particularly <hi type="italic">declare thy mighty acts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.3">Ps. lxxviii. 3</reference>); and the generation that is rising up shall follow the example of that which is going off: so that the death of God's worshippers shall be no diminution of his worship, for a new generation shall rise up in their room to carry on that good work, more or less, to the end of time, when it shall be left to that world to do it in which there is no succession of generations. <div eID="gen13232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13233" type="x-p"/> II. What we must give to God the glory of. <div eID="gen13233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13234" type="x-p"/> 1. Of his greatness and his great works. We must declare, <hi type="italic">Great is the Lord,</hi> his presence infinite, his power irresistible, his brightness insupportable, his majesty awful, his dominion boundless, and his sovereignty incontestable; and therefore there is no dispute, but <hi type="italic">great is the Lord, and,</hi> if great, then <hi type="italic">greatly to be praised,</hi> with all that is within us, to the utmost of our power, and with all the circumstances of solemnity imaginable. His greatness indeed cannot be comprehended, for it is unsearchable; who can conceive or express how great God is? But then it is so much the more to be praised. When we cannot, by searching, find the bottom, we must sit down at the brink, and adore the depth, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Rom. xi. 33</reference>. God is great, for, (1.) His majesty is glorious in the upper world, above the heavens, where he has set his glory; and when we are declaring his greatness we must not fail to <hi type="italic">speak of the glorious honour of his majesty,</hi> the splendour of the glory of his majesty (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.5">v. 5</reference>), how brightly he shines in the upper world, so as to dazzle the eyes of the angels themselves, and oblige them to cover their faces, as unable to bear the lustre of it. (2.) His works are wondrous in this lower world. The preservation, maintenance, and government of all the creatures, proclaim the Creator very great. When therefore we declare his greatness we must observe the unquestionable proofs of it, and must <hi type="italic">declare his mighty acts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">speak of his wondrous works</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">the might of his terrible acts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.145.6">v. 6</reference>. We must see God acting and working in all the affairs of this lower world. Various instruments are used, but in all events God is the supreme director; it is he that performs all things. Much of his power is seen in the operations of his providence (they are <hi type="italic">mighty acts,</hi> such as cannot be paralleled by the strength of any creature), and much of his justice—they are <hi type="italic">terrible acts,</hi> awful to saints, dreadful to sinners. These we should take all occasions to speak of, observing the finger of God, his hand, his arm, in all, that we may marvel. <div eID="gen13234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13235" type="x-p"/> 2. Of his goodness; this is his glory, <reference osisRef="Exod.33.19">Exod. xxxiii. 19</reference>. It is what he glories in (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.6-Exod.34.7">Exod. xxxiv. 6, 7</reference>), and it is what we must give him the glory of: <hi type="italic">They shall abundantly utter the memory of thy great goodness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.145.7">v. 7</reference>. God's goodness is great goodness, the treasures of it can never be exhausted, nay, they can never be lessened, for he ever will be as rich in mercy as he ever was. It is memorable goodness; it is what we ought always to lay before us, always to have in mind and preserve the memorials of, for it is <hi type="italic">worthy to be had in everlasting remembrance;</hi> and the remembrance we retain of God's goodness we should utter, we should <hi type="italic">abundantly utter,</hi> as those who are full of it, very full of it, and desire that others may be acquainted and affected with it. But, whenever we utter God's great goodness, we must not forget, at the same time, to <hi type="italic">sing of his righteousness;</hi> for, as he is gracious in rewarding those that serve him faithfully, so he is righteous in punishing those that rebel against him. Impartial and inflexible justice is as surely in God as inexhaustible goodness; and we must sing of both together, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.22">Rom. xi. 22</reference>. (1.) There is a fountain of goodness in God's nature (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord is gracious</hi> to those that serve him; he is <hi type="italic">full of compassion</hi> to those that need him, <hi type="italic">slow to anger</hi> to those that have offended him, <hi type="italic">and of great mercy</hi> to all that seek him and sue to him. He is ready to give, and ready to forgive, more ready than we are to ask, than we are to repent. (2.) There are streams of goodness in all the dispensations of his providence, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.9">v. 9</reference>. As he is good, so he does good; he <hi type="italic">is good to all,</hi> to all his creatures, from the highest angel to the meanest worm, to all but devils and damned sinners, that have shut themselves out from his goodness. <hi type="italic">His tender mercies are over all his works.</hi> [1.] All his works, all his creatures, receive the fruits of his merciful care and bounty. It is extended to them all; he hates nothing that he has made. [2.] The works of his mercy out-shine all his other works, and declare him more than any of them. In nothing will the glory of God be for ever so illustrious as in the vessels of mercy ordained to glory. To the divine goodness will the everlasting hallelujahs of all the saints be sung.
entries.497746c8d9d97185fea0ebe584bece803c2d541f: <div eID="gen13235" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Grateful Acknowledgments.</title> <div sID="gen13236" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> All thy works shall praise thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ; and thy saints shall bless thee. <hi type="super">11</hi> They shall speak of the glory of thy kingdom, and talk of thy power; <hi type="super">12</hi> To make known to the sons of men his mighty acts, and the glorious majesty of his kingdom. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thy kingdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> an everlasting kingdom, and thy dominion <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> throughout all generations. <hi type="super">14</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all <hi type="italic">those that be</hi> bowed down. <hi type="super">15</hi> The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season. <hi type="super">16</hi> Thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing. <hi type="super">17</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works. <hi type="super">18</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> nigh unto all them that call upon him, to all that call upon him in truth. <hi type="super">19</hi> He will fulfil the desire of them that fear him: he also will hear their cry, and will save them. <hi type="super">20</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy. <hi type="super">21</hi> My mouth shall speak the praise of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and let all flesh bless his holy name for ever and ever. <div eID="gen13236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13237" type="x-p"/> The greatness and goodness of him who is <hi type="italic">optimus et maximus</hi>—<hi type="italic">the best and greatest</hi> of beings, were celebrated in the former part of the psalm; here, in these verses, we are taught to give him <hi type="italic">the glory of his kingdom,</hi> in the administration of which his greatness and goodness shine so clearly, so very brightly. Observe, as before, <div eID="gen13237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13238" type="x-p"/> I. From whom the tribute of praise is expected (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">All</hi> God's <hi type="italic">works shall praise</hi> him. They all minister to us matter for praise, and so praise him according to their capacity; even those that refuse to give him honour he will get himself honour upon. But his <hi type="italic">saints</hi> do <hi type="italic">bless</hi> him, not only as they have peculiar blessings from him, which other creatures have not, but as they praise him actively, while his other works praise him only objectively. They bless him, for they collect the rent or tribute of praise from the inferior creatures, and pay it into the treasury above. All God's works do praise him, as the beautiful building praises the builder or the well-drawn picture praises the painter; but the saints bless him as the children of prudent tender parents rise up and call them blessed. Of all God's works, his saints, the workmanship of his grace, the first-fruits of his creatures, have most reason to bless him. <div eID="gen13238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13239" type="x-p"/> II. For what this praise is to be given: <hi type="italic">They shall speak of thy kingdom.</hi> The kingdom of God among men is a thing to be often thought of and often spoken of. As, before, he had magnified God's greatness and goodness in general, so here he magnifies them with application to his kingdom. Consider then, <div eID="gen13239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13240" type="x-p"/> 1. The greatness of his kingdom. It is great indeed, for all the kings and kingdoms of the earth are under his control. To show the greatness of God's kingdom, he observes, (1.) The pomp of it. Would we by faith look within the veil, we should see, and, believing, we should <hi type="italic">speak of the glory of his kingdom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">the glorious majesty of</hi> it (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.12">v. 12</reference>), for he has prepared his throne in the heavens, and it is high and lifted up, and surrounded with an innumerable company of angels. The courts of Solomon and Ahasuerus were magnificent; but, compared with the glorious majesty of God's kingdom, they were but as glow-worms to the sun. The consideration of this should strike an awe upon us in all our approaches to God. (2.) The power of it: When <hi type="italic">they speak of the glory of</hi> God's <hi type="italic">kingdom</hi> they must <hi type="italic">talk of</hi> his <hi type="italic">power,</hi> the extent of it, the efficacy of it—his power, by which he can do any thing and does every thing he pleases (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.11">v. 11</reference>); and, as a proof of it, let them <hi type="italic">make known his mighty acts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.12">v. 12</reference>), that <hi type="italic">the sons of men</hi> may be invited to yield themselves his willing subjects and so put themselves under the protection of such a mighty potentate. (3.) The perpetuity of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.13">v. 13</reference>. The thrones of earthly princes totter, and the flowers of their crowns wither, monarchies come to an end; but, Lord, <hi type="italic">thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom.</hi> God will govern the world to the end of time, when the Mediator, who is now entrusted with the administration of his kingdom, shall deliver it up to God, even the Father, that he may be all in all to eternity. His <hi type="italic">dominion endures throughout all generations,</hi> for he himself is eternal, and his counsels are unchangeable and uniform; and Satan, who has set up a kingdom in opposition to him, is conquered and in a chain. <div eID="gen13240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13241" type="x-p"/> 2. The goodness of his kingdom. His royal style and title are, <hi type="italic">The Lord God, gracious and merciful;</hi> and his government answers to his title. The goodness of God appears in what he does, <div eID="gen13241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13242" type="x-p"/> (1.) For all the creatures in general (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.15-Ps.145.16">v. 15, 16</reference>): He <hi type="italic">provides food for all flesh,</hi> and therein appears his everlasting mercy, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.25">Ps. cxxxvi. 25</reference>. All the creatures live upon God, and, as they had their being from him at first, so from him they have all the supports of their being and on him they depend for the continuance of it. [1.] The eye of their expectation attends upon him: <hi type="italic">The eyes of all wait on thee.</hi> The inferior creatures indeed have not the knowledge of God, nor are capable of it, and yet they are said to <hi type="italic">wait upon God,</hi> because they seek their food according to the instinct which the God of nature has put into them (and <hi type="italic">they sow not, neither do they reap,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.26">Matt. vi. 26</reference>), and because they take what the God of nature has provided for them, in the time and way that he has appointed, and are content with it. [2.] The hand of his bounty is stretched out to them: <hi type="italic">Thou givest them their meat in due season,</hi> the meat proper for them, and in the proper time, when they need it; so that none of the creatures ordinarily perish for want of food, no, not in the winter. <hi type="italic">Thou openest thy hand</hi> freely and liberally, <hi type="italic">and satisfiest the desire of every living thing,</hi> except some of the unreasonable children of men, that will be satisfied with nothing, but are still complaining, still crying, <hi type="italic">Give, give.</hi> <div eID="gen13242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13243" type="x-p"/> (2.) For the children of men in particular, whom he governs as reasonable creatures. <div eID="gen13243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13244" type="x-p"/> [1.] He does none of them any wrong, for (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.17">v. 17</reference>) <hi type="italic">the Lord is righteous in all his ways,</hi> and not unrighteous in any of them; he is <hi type="italic">holy,</hi> and acts like himself, with a perfect rectitude <hi type="italic">in all his works.</hi> In all the acts of government he is just, injurious to none, but administering justice to all. <hi type="italic">The ways of the lord are equal,</hi> though ours are unequal. In giving laws, in deciding controversies, in recompensing services, and punishing offences, he is incontestably just, and we are bound to own that he is so. <div eID="gen13244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13245" type="x-p"/> [2.] He does all of them good, his own people in a special manner. <div eID="gen13245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13246" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He supports those that are sinking, and it is his honour to help the weak, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.14">v. 14</reference>. He <hi type="italic">upholds all that fall,</hi> in that, though they fall, they are not utterly cast down. Many of the children of men are brought very low by sickness and other distresses, and seem ready to drop into the grave, and yet Providence wonderfully upholds them, raises them up, and says, <hi type="italic">Return,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>. If all had died who once seemed dying, the world would have been very thin. Many of the children of God, who have been ready to fall into sin, to fall into despair, have experienced his goodness in preventing their falls, or recovering them speedily by his graces and comforts, so that, though they fell, they were <hi type="italic">not utterly cast down,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.24">Ps. xxxvii. 24</reference>. If those who were <hi type="italic">bowed down</hi> by oppression and affliction are <hi type="italic">raised up,</hi> it was God that raised them. And, with respect to all those <hi type="italic">that are heavy-laden</hi> under the burden of sin, if they come to Christ by faith, he will ease them, he will raise them. <div eID="gen13246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13247" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He is very ready to hear and answer the prayers of his people, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.18-Ps.145.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. In this appears the grace of his kingdom, that his subjects have not only liberty of petitioning, but all the encouragement that can be to petition. 1. The grant is very rich, that God will be <hi type="italic">nigh to all that call upon him;</hi> he will be always within call of their prayers, and they shall always find themselves within reach of his help. If <hi type="italic">a neighbour that is near is better than a brother afar off</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.10">Prov. xxvii. 10</reference>), much more a God that is near. Nay, he will not only be <hi type="italic">nigh to them,</hi> that they may have the satisfaction of being heard, but <hi type="italic">he will fulfil</hi> their <hi type="italic">desires;</hi> they shall have what they ask and find that they seek. It was said (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.16">v. 16</reference>) that he <hi type="italic">satisfies the desire of every living thing,</hi> much more <hi type="italic">will he fulfil the desire of those that fear him;</hi> for he that feeds his birds will not starve his babes. <hi type="italic">He will hear their call and will save them;</hi> that is hearing them to purpose, as he heard David (that is, saved him) <hi type="italic">from the horn of the unicorn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.22.21">Ps. xxii. 21</reference>. 2. The proviso is very reasonable. He will hear and help us, (1.) If we <hi type="italic">fear him,</hi> if we worship and serve him with a holy awe of him; for otherwise how can we expect that he should accept us? (2.) If we <hi type="italic">call upon him in truth;</hi> for he desires truth in the inward part. We must be faithful to God, and sincere in our professions of dependence on him, and devotedness to him. In all devotions inward impressions must be answerable to the outward expressions, else they are not performed in truth. <div eID="gen13247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13248" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He takes those under his special protection who have a confidence and complacency in him (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord preserves all those that love him;</hi> they lie exposed in this world, but he, by preserving them in their integrity, will effectually secure them, that no real evil shall befal them. <div eID="gen13248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13249" type="x-p"/> [3.] If any are destroyed they may thank themselves: <hi type="italic">All the wicked he will destroy,</hi> but they have by their wickedness fitted themselves for destruction. This magnifies his goodness in the protection of the righteous, that <hi type="italic">with their eyes they shall see the reward of the wicked</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.8">Ps. xci. 8</reference>); and God will by this means preserve his people, even by destroying the wicked that would do them a mischief. <div eID="gen13249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13250" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The psalmist concludes, 1. With a resolution to give glory to God himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord.</hi> When we have said what we can, in praising God, still there is more to be said, and therefore we must not only begin our thanksgivings with this purpose, as he did (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.1">v. 1</reference>), but conclude them with it, as he does here, because we shall presently have occasion to begin again. As the end of one mercy is the beginning of another, so should the end of one thanksgiving be. While I have breath to draw, my mouth shall still speak God's praises. 2. With a call to others to do so too: <hi type="italic">Let all flesh,</hi> all mankind, <hi type="italic">bless his holy name for ever and ever.</hi> Some of mankind shall be blessing God for ever; it is a pity but that they should be all so engaged.  <chapter eID="Ps.145"/> <div eID="gen13250" type="x-p"/>

entries.751946f82580bca31edd8e3cf08fd125507c5b35: <div eID="gen23474" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23475" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23476" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23476" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23475" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23477" type="x-p"/> God is praised for his unsearchable greatness, <reference osisRef="Psa.145.1">Psa 145:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.145.2">Psa 145:2</reference>; for his majesty and terrible acts, <reference osisRef="Psa.145.3">Psa 145:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.145.6">Psa 145:6</reference>; for his goodness and tender mercies to all, <reference osisRef="Psa.145.7-Psa.145.9">Psa 145:7-9</reference>; for his power and kingdom, <reference osisRef="Psa.145.10-Psa.145.13">Psa 145:10-13</reference>; for his kindness to the distressed, <reference osisRef="Psa.145.14">Psa 145:14</reference>; for his providence, <reference osisRef="Psa.145.15-Psa.145.17">Psa 145:15-17</reference>. He hears and answers prayer, <reference osisRef="Psa.145.18-Psa.145.20">Psa 145:18-20</reference>. All should praise him, <reference osisRef="Psa.145.21">Psa 145:21</reference>. <div eID="gen23477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23478" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is attributed to David by the Hebrew and all the Versions. It is the last of the acrostic Psalms; and should contain twenty-two verses, as answering to the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet; but the verse between the thirteenth and fourteenth, beginning with the letter נ nun, is lost out of the present Hebrew copies; but a translation of it is found in the Syriac, Septuagint, Vulgate, Ethiopic, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon. See below. It is an incomparable Psalm of praise; and the rabbins have it in such high estimation, that they assert, if a man with sincerity of heart repeat it three times a-day, he shall infallibly enjoy the blessings of the world to come. It does not appear on what particular occasion it was composed; or, indeed, whether there was any occasion but gratitude to God for his ineffable favors to mankind. <div eID="gen23478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23479" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23480" type="x-p"/> I will extol thee - I will raise thee on high, I will lift thee up. <div eID="gen23480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23481" type="x-p"/> I will bless thy name - לעולם ועד leolam vaed, for ever and onward, in this and the coming world. This sort of expressions, which are very difficult to be translated, are on the whole well expressed by those words, in a hymn of Mr. Addison: - <div eID="gen23481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23482" type="x-p"/> Through all eternity to theeA joyful song I'll raise <div eID="gen23482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23483" type="x-p"/> But O, eternity's too shortTo utter all thy praise! <div eID="gen23483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23484" type="x-p"/> This contains a strong hyperbole; but allowable in such cases.
entries.f8caeb07dd4a28a056092ab6198714dc1050f475: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23485" type="x-p"/> His greatness is unsearchable - Literally, To his mightinesses there is no investigation. All in God is unlimited and eternal.
entries.048c4848489341f9c4bb0d3918b777f54daa59bc: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23486" type="x-p"/> One generation - Thy creating and redeeming acts are recorded in thy word; but thy wondrous providential dealings with mankind must be handed down by tradition, from generation to generation; for they are in continual occurrence, and consequently innumerable.
entries.734b4b4200c8fa1717c0e3ef5ffd18ed64d9e4d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23487" type="x-p"/> The Lord is gracious - His holy nature is ever disposed to show favor. <div eID="gen23487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23488" type="x-p"/> Full of compassion - Wherever he sees misery, his eye affects his heart. <div eID="gen23488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23489" type="x-p"/> Slow to anger - When there is even the greatest provocation. <div eID="gen23489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23490" type="x-p"/> Of great mercy - Great in his abundant mercy. These four things give us a wonderful display of the goodness of the Divine nature.
entries.8690ac92b8c01543f2a8b58f9297f1c68f086e2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen23490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23491" type="x-p"/> The Lord is good to all - There is not a soul out of hell that is not continually under his most merciful regards; so far is he from willing or decreeing before their creation the damnation of any man. <div eID="gen23491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23492" type="x-p"/> His tender mercies - His bowels of compassion are over all his works; he feels for his intelligent offspring, as the most affectionate mother does for the child of her own bosom. And through this matchless mercy, these bowels of compassion, his son Jesus tasted death for every man. How far is all that is here spoken of the nature of God opposed to the Molochian doctrine of the eternal decree of reprobation! "His grace for every soul is free: <div eID="gen23492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23493" type="x-p"/> For his, who forged the dire decree; <div eID="gen23493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23494" type="x-p"/> For every reprobate and me."
entries.638e96a6ce07b14a87ec3f98f13dff4b7d2dbe01: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23495" type="x-p"/> All thy works shall praise thee - The God who is good to all. <div eID="gen23495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23496" type="x-p"/> Thy saints - חסידיך chasideycha, thy compassionate ones; those who are partakers of thy great mercy, <reference osisRef="Psa.145.8">Psa 145:8</reference>. These shall bless thee, because they know, they feel, that thou willest the salvation of all. The dark, the gloomy, the hard-hearted, the narrow-minded bigots, who never have had thy love shed abroad in their hearts, can unfeelingly deal in the damnation of their fellows.
entries.421644e5b2c6e8f7d2af0b35be4e58cf580720d4: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen23496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23497" type="x-p"/> To make known - They delight to recommend their God and Father to others.
entries.e0c89a15e09e6b5116a243ba5c7a3594a7a8d0d4: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen23497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23498" type="x-p"/> Thy dominion endureth - There is neither age nor people in and over which God does not manifest his benignly ruling power. As the above verse begins with the letter מ mem, the next in the order of the alphabet shouid begin with נ nun: but that verse is totally wanting. To say it never was in, is false, because the alphabet is not complete without it; and it is an unanswerable argument to prove the careless manner in which the Jews have preserved the Divine records. Though the Syriac, Septuagint, Vulgate, Ethiopic, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon, have a verse, not in the Hebrew text, that answers to the נ nun, which is found in no printed copy of the Hebrew Bible; yet one MS., now in Trinity College, Dublin, has it thus, I suppose by correction, in the bottom of the page: - נאמן יהוה בכל דבריו וחסיד בכל מעשיו <div eID="gen23498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23499" type="x-p"/> Neeman Yehovah bechol debaraiv; vechasid bechol maasaiv. "The Lord is faithful in all his words; and merciful in all his works." Πιστος Κυριος εν τοις λογοις αυτου· και ὁσιος εν πασι τιος εργοις αυτου. - Septuagint. <div eID="gen23499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23500" type="x-p"/> Fidelis Dominus in omnibus verbis suis: et sanctus in omnibus operibus suis - Vulgate. <div eID="gen23500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23501" type="x-p"/> These two Versions, the Septuagint and Vulgate, are the same with the Hebrew given above. The Anglo-Saxon is the same: - "True Lord in all words his, and holy in all works his." <div eID="gen23501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23502" type="x-p"/> The Latin text in my old Psalter is the same with the present printed Vulgate: "Fidelis Dominus in omnibus verbis suis, et sanctus in omnibus operibus suis." <div eID="gen23502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23503" type="x-p"/> Thus translated in the same MSS.: Lorde true in all his words: and holy in al his workes. <div eID="gen23503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23504" type="x-p"/> It is remarkable that the whole verse is wanting in the Vulgate, as published in the Complutenstan Polyglot, as also the Antwerp and Paris Polyglots, which were taken from it. It is wanting also in the Polyglot Psalter of Porus, because he did not find it in the Hebrew text.
entries.166090777fe2db17fe26a70da4c6331c66f8909f: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen23504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23505" type="x-p"/> The Lord upholdeth all that fall - נפלים nophelim, the falling, or those who are not able to keep their feet; the weak. He shores them up; he is their prop. No man falls through his own weakness merely; if he rely on God, the strongest foe cannot shake him.
entries.fa6de4201e438fa10357a7c3becca9b7cb50b949: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen23505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23506" type="x-p"/> The eyes of all wait upon thee - What a fine figure! The young of all animals look up to their parents for food. God is here represented as the universal Father, providing food for every living creature. <div eID="gen23506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23507" type="x-p"/> In due season - The kind of food that is suited to every animal, and to all the stages of life in each animal. This is a wonderful mystery. It is a fact that all are thus provided for; but how is it done? All expect it from God, and not one is dsappointed! For,
entries.8d92c83135d04422d05521a0a7991376549a639a: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen23507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23508" type="x-p"/> Thou openest thine hand - What a hand is this that holds in it all the food that meets the desires and necessities of the universe of creatures! A very large volume might be written upon this: The proper kinds of food for the various classes of animals.
entries.f106ef90be2d68901332ddd12d96f0d76de87541: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen23508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23509" type="x-p"/> The Lord is righteous - It was the similarity of this to the omitted verse, which should have been the fourteenth, that caused it to be omitted.
entries.09d31598a3c8c4e066c62cac946d0668c28e4610: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen23509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23510" type="x-p"/> The Lord is nigh - Whoever calls upon God in truth, with a sincere and upright heart, one that truly desires his salvation, to that person God is nigh. The following verse shows he is not only near to praying people, but <div eID="gen23510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23511" type="x-p"/> 1. He will hear their cry. <div eID="gen23511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23512" type="x-p"/> 2. Fulfil their desires. <div eID="gen23512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23513" type="x-p"/> 3. Save them. Reader, lift up thy soul in prayer to this merciful God.
entries.a263f73205af640fa0063c046c34c7a2e55aad79: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen23513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23514" type="x-p"/> The Lord preserveth - He is the keeper of all them that love him. <div eID="gen23514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23515" type="x-p"/> But all the wicked will he destroy - They call not upon him; they fight against him, and he will confound and destroy them. There is something curious in the שומר shomer, the keeper or guardian of the pious; he is שמיד shamid, the destroyer of the wicked. The first word implies he is continually keeping them; the second, that he causes the others to be destroyed.
entries.b6e18b9913c12f7585f6fccb1cc623e305be384f: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen23515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23516" type="x-p"/> Let all flesh bless his holy name - He is good to all, wants to save all, actually feeds and preserves all. And as near as שמר shamar is to שמד shamad, so near is he a Savior to those who stand on the brink of destruction, if they will look to him. <div eID="gen23516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23517" type="x-p"/> For the application of all this Psalm to the Church of Christ, see the analysis.  <chapter eID="Ps.145"/> <div eID="gen23517" type="x-p"/>

entries.511901cfffa08fc68ec86ef231dce2a8c8c7372b: <div eID="gen10323" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Hymn in Praise of the All-Bountiful King</title> <div sID="gen10324" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Ps.144.1-Ps.144.15">Psa 144:1-15</reference> the collection draws doxologically towards its close. This Psalm, which begins in the form of the <hi type="italic">beracha</hi> (ברוך ה), is followed by another in which <hi type="italic">benedicam</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.1-Ps.145.2">Psa 145:1-2</reference>) and <hi type="italic">benedicat</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.21">Psa 145:21</reference>) is the favourite word. It is the only Psalm that bears the title תּהלּה, whose plural תּהלּים is become the collective name of the Psalms. In <hi type="italic">B.</hi> Berachoth 4 <hi type="italic">b</hi> it is distinguished by the apophthegm: “Every one who repeats the תהלה לדוד three times a day may be sure that he is a child of the world to come (בן העולם הבא).” And why? Not merely because this Psalm, as the Gemara says, אתיא באלף בית, i.e., follows the course of the alphabet (for Ps 119 is in fact also alphabetical, and that in an eightfold degree), and not merely because it celebrates God’s care for all creatures (for this the Great Hallel also does, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.25">Psa 136:25</reference>), but because it unites both these prominent qualities in itself (משׁום דאית ביה תרתי). In fact, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.16">Psa 145:16</reference> is a celebration of the goodness of God which embraces every living thing, with which only <reference osisRef="Ps.136.25">Psa 136:25</reference>, and not <reference osisRef="Ps.111.5">Psa 111:5</reference>, can be compared. <hi type="italic">Valde sententiosus hic Psalmus est</hi>, says Bakius; and do we not find in this Psalm our favourite <hi type="italic">Benedicite</hi> and <hi type="italic">Oculi omnium</hi> which our children repeat before a meal? It is the ancient church’s Psalm for the noon-day repast (vid., Armknecht, <hi type="italic">Die heilige Psalmodie</hi>, 1855, S. 54); <reference osisRef="Ps.145.15">Psa 145:15</reference> was also used at the holy communion, hence Chrysostom says it contains τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα, ἅπερ οἱ μεμυημένοι συνεχῶς ὑποψάλλουσι λέγοντες· Οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ πάντων εἰς σὲ ἐλπίζουσιν καὶ σὺ δίδως τὴν τροφὴν αὐτῶν ἐν εὐκαιρίᾳ. Κατὰ στοιχεῖον, observes Theodoret, καὶ οὗτος ὁ ὕμνος σύγκειται. The Psalm is distichic, and every first line of the distich has the ordinal letter; but the distich <hi type="italic">Nun</hi> is wanting. The Talmud (<hi type="italic">loc cit.</hi>) is of opinion that it is because the fatal נפלה (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.2">Amo 5:2</reference>), which David, going on at once with סומך ה לכל־הנפלים, skips over, begins with <hi type="italic">Nun</hi>. On the other hand, Ewald, Vaihinger, and Sommer, like Grotius, think that the <hi type="italic">Nun</hi>-strophe has been lost. The lxx (but not Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, nor Jerome in his translation after the original text) gives such a strophe, perhaps out of a MS (like the Dublin <hi type="italic">Cod. Kennicot</hi>, 142) in which it was supplied: Πιστὸς (נאמן as in <reference osisRef="Ps.111.7">Psa 111:7</reference>) κύριος ἐν (πᾶσι) τοῖς λόγοις αὐτοῦ καὶ ὅσιος ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ (according with <reference osisRef="Ps.145.17">Psa 145:17</reference>, with the change only of two words of this distich). Hitzig is of opinion that the original <hi type="italic">Nun</hi>-strophe has been welded into <reference osisRef="Ps.141.1-Ps.141.10">Psa 141:1-10</reference>; but only his clairvoyant-like historical discernment is able to amalgamate <reference osisRef="Ps.145.6">Psa 145:6</reference> of this Psalm with our Psalms 145. We are contented to see in the omission of the <hi type="italic">Nun</hi>-strophe an example of that freedom with which the Old Testament poets are wont to handle this kind of forms. Likewise there is no reason apparent for there fact that Jeremiah has chosen in <reference osisRef="Lam.2.1">Lam 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.1">Lam 3:1</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Lam.4.1">Lam 4:1</reference> of the Lamentations to make the <hi type="italic">Ajin</hi>-strophe follow the <hi type="italic">Pe</hi>-strophe three times, whilst in <reference osisRef="Lam.1.1">Lam 1:1</reference> it precedes it.
entries.60b26072abee3f350e96aed6e99cf3ae262b534f: <reference osisRef="Ps.145.1-Ps.145.7">Psa 145:1-7</reference> <div eID="gen10324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10325" type="x-p"/> The strains with which this hymn opens are familiar Psalm-strains. We are reminded of <reference osisRef="Ps.30.2">Psa 30:2</reference>, and the likewise alphabetical song of praise and thanksgiving Psa 34:2. The <hi type="italic">plena scriptio</hi> אלוהי in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.10">Psa 143:10</reference>; Psa 98:6. The language of address “my God the King,” which sounds harsh in comparison with the otherwise usual “my King and my God” (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.3">Psa 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.4">Psa 84:4</reference>), purposely calls God with unrelated generality, that is to say in the most absolute manner, the King. If the poet is himself a king, the occasion for this appellation of God is all the more natural and the signification all the more pertinent. But even in the mouth of any other person it is significant. Whosoever calls God by such a name acknowledges His royal prerogative, and at the same time does homage to Him and binds himself to allegiance; and it is just this confessory act of exalting Him who in Himself is the absolutely lofty One that is here called רומם. But who can the poet express the purpose of praising God’s Name <hi type="italic">for ever</hi>? Because the praise of God is a need of his inmost nature, he has a perfect right to forget his own mortality when engaged upon this devotion to the ever-living King. Clinging adoringly to the Eternal One, he must seem to himself to be eternal; and if there is a practical proof for a life after death, it is just this ardent desire of the soul, wrought of God Himself, after the praise of the God of its life (lit., its origin) which affords it the highest, noblest delight. The idea of the silent Hades, which forces itself forward elsewhere, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.6.6">Psa 6:6</reference>, where the mind of the poet is beclouded by sin, is here entirely removed, inasmuch as here the mind of the poet is the undimmed mirror of the divine glory. Therefore <reference osisRef="Ps.145.2">Psa 145:2</reference> also does not concede the possibility of any interruption of the praise: the poet will daily (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.20">Psa 68:20</reference>) bless God, be they days of prosperity or of sorrow, uninterruptedly in all eternity will he glorify His Name (אהללה as in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.31">Psa 69:31</reference>). There is no worthier and more exhaustless object of praise (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.3">Psa 145:3</reference>): Jahve is great, and greatly to be praised (מהלּל, taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Psa 48:2</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.96.4">Psa 96:4</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.18.4">Psa 18:4</reference>), and of His “greatness” (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.11">1Ch 29:11</reference>, where this attribute precedes all others) there is no searching out, i.e., it is so abysmally deep that no searching can reach its bottom (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.28">Isa 40:28</reference>; Job 11:7.). It has, however, been revealed, and is being revealed continually, and is for this very reason thus celebrated in <reference osisRef="Ps.145.4">Psa 145:4</reference> : one generation propagates to the next the growing praise of the works that He has wrought out (עשׂה מעשׁים), and men are able to relate all manner of proofs of His victorious power which prevails over everything, and makes everything subject to itself (גּבוּרת as in <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>, and frequently). This historically manifest and traditional divine doxa and the facts (דּברי as in <reference osisRef="Ps.105.27">Psa 105:27</reference>) of the divine wonders the poet will devoutly consider. הדר stands in attributive relation to כּבוד, as this on its part does to הודך. Thy brilliantly gloriously (kingly) majesty (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.22.18">Jer 22:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.21">Dan 11:21</reference>). The poet does not say גּם אני, nor may we insert it, either here in <reference osisRef="Ps.145.5">Psa 145:5</reference>, or in <reference osisRef="Ps.145.6">Psa 145:6</reference>, where the same sequence of thoughts recurs, more briefly expressed. The emphasis lies on the objects. The mightiness (עזוּז as in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.4">Psa 78:4</reference>, and in <reference osisRef="Isa.42.25">Isa 42:25</reference>, where it signifies violence) of His terrible acts shall pass from mouth to mouth (אמר with a substantival object as in <reference osisRef="Ps.40.11">Psa 40:11</reference>), and His mighty acts (גּדלּות, <hi type="italic">magnalia</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.17.19">1Ch 17:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.17.21">1Ch 17:21</reference>) - according to the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> (which is determined by the suffix of אספּרנּה; cf. however, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.23">2Sa 22:23</reference>; 2Ki 3:3; 2Ki 10:26, and frequently): His greatness (גּדלּה) - will he also on his part make the matter of his narrating. It is, however, not alone the awe-inspiring majesty of God which is revealed in history, but also the greatness (רב used as a substantive as in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.20">Psa 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.7">Isa 63:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.7">Isa 21:7</reference>, whereas רבּים in <reference osisRef="Ps.32.10">Psa 32:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.51">Psa 89:51</reference> is an adjective placed before the noun after the manner of a numeral), i.e., the abundant measure, of His goodness and His righteousness, i.e., His acting in inviolable correspondence with His counsel and order of salvation. The memory of the transcendent goodness of God is the object of universal, overflowing acknowledgement and the righteousness of God is the object of universal exultation (רנּן with the accusative as in <reference osisRef="Ps.51.16">Psa 51:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.59.17">Psa 59:17</reference>). After the poet has sung the glorious self-attestation of God according to both its sides, the fiery and the light sides, he lingers by the light side, the front side of the Name of Jahve unfolded in Exo 34:6.
entries.53dc40ea6c0165c5bfc027a576f314b0fcf336d9: <reference osisRef="Ps.145.8-Ps.145.13">Psa 145:8-13</reference> <div eID="gen10325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10326" type="x-p"/> This memorable utterance of Jahve concerning Himself the writer of Ps 103, which is of kindred import, also interweaves into his celebration of the revelation of divine love in Psa 145:8. Instead of רב־חסד the expression here, however, is וגדול חסד (<hi type="italic">Kerî</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Nah.1.3">Nah 1:3</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.89.29">Psa 89:29</reference>, with <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi> וּגדל־). The real will of God tends towards favour, which gladly giving stoops to give (חנּוּן), and towards compassion, which interests itself on behalf of the sinner for his help and comfort (רחוּם). Wrath is only the background of His nature, which He reluctantly and only after long waiting (ארך אפּים) lets loose against those who spurn His great mercy. For His goodness embraces, as <reference osisRef="Ps.145.9">Psa 145:9</reference> says, all; His tender mercies are over all His works, they hover over and encompass all His creatures. Therefore, too, all His works praise Him: they are all together loud-speaking witnesses of that sympathetic all-embracing love of His, which excludes no one who does not exclude himself; and His saints, who live in God’s love, bless Him (יברכוּכה written as in 1Ki 18:44): their mouth overflows with the declaration (יאמרוּ) of the glory of the kingdom of this loving God, and in speaking (ידבּרוּ) of the sovereign power with which He maintains and extends this kingdom. This confession they make their employ, in order that the knowledge of the mighty acts of God and the glorious majesty of His kingdom may at length become the general possession of mankind. When the poet in <reference osisRef="Ps.145.12">Psa 145:12</reference> sets forth the purpose of the proclamation, he drops the form of address. God’s kingdom is a kingdom of all aeons, and His dominion is manifested without exception and continually in all periods or generations (בּכל־דּור ודר as in Ps 45:18, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.28">Est 9:28</reference>, a pleonastic strengthening of the expression בּדר ודר, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1">Psa 90:1</reference>). It is the eternal circumference of the history of time, but at the same time its eternal substance, which more and more unfolds and achieves itself in the succession of the periods that mark its course. For that all things in heaven and on earth shall be gathered up together (ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Eph 1:10</reference>) in the all-embracing kingdom of God in His Christ, is the goal of all history, and therefore the substance of history which is working itself out. With <reference osisRef="Ps.145.13">Psa 145:13</reference> (cf. Dan. 3:33, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.31">Dan 4:31</reference>, according to Hitzig the primary passages) another paragraph is brought to a close.
entries.ee4b97e01df59ab7dfcf18ca42ef6b0900c2e1da: <reference osisRef="Ps.145.14-Ps.145.21">Psa 145:14-21</reference> <div eID="gen10326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10327" type="x-p"/> The poet now celebrates in detail the deeds of the gracious King. The words with ל are pure datives, cf. the accusative expression in Psa 146:8. He in person is the support which holds fast the falling ones (נופלים, here not the fallen ones, see <reference osisRef="Ps.28.1">Psa 28:1</reference>) in the midst of falling (Nicephorus: τοὺς καταπεσεῖν μέλλοντας ἑδραιοῖ, ὥστε μὴ καταπεσεῖν), and the stay by which those who are bowed together raise themselves. He is the Provider for all beings, the Father of the house, to whom in the great house of the world the eyes (עיני with the second <hi type="italic">ê</hi> toneless, Ew. §100, b) of all beings, endowed with reason and irrational, are directed with calm confidence (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.26">Mat 6:26</reference>), and who gives them their food in its, i.e., in due season. The language of <reference osisRef="Ps.104.27">Psa 104:27</reference> is very similar, and it proceeds here, too, as there in <reference osisRef="Ps.104.28">Psa 104:28</reference> (cf. Sir. 40:14). He opens His hand, which is ever full, much as a man who feeds the doves in his court does, and gives רצון, pleasure, i.e., that which is good, which is the fulfilling of their desire, in sufficient fulness to all living things (and therefore those in need of support for the body and the life). Thus it is to be interpreted, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.33.23">Deu 33:23</reference> (after which here in the lxx the reading varies between εὐδοκίας and εὐλογίας), cf. <reference osisRef="Acts.14.17">Act 14:17</reference>, ἐμπιπλών τροφῆς καὶ εὐφροσύνης τάς καρδίας ἡμῶν. השׂבּיע is construed with a dative and accusative of the object instead of with two accusatives of the object (Ges. §139. 1, 2). The usage of the language is unacquainted with רצון as an adverb in the sense of “willingly” (Hitzig), which would rather be ברצונך. In all the ways that Jahve takes in His historical rule He is “righteous,” i.e., He keeps strictly to the rule (norm) of His holy love; and in all His works which He accomplishes in the course of history He is merciful (חסיד), i.e., He practises mercy (חסד, see <reference osisRef="Ps.12.2">Psa 12:2</reference>); for during the present time of mercy the primary essence of His active manifestation is free preventing mercy, condescending love. True, He remains at a distance from the hypocrites, just as their heart remains far from Him (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.13">Isa 29:13</reference>); but as for the rest, with impartial equality He is nigh (קרוב as in <reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">Psa 34:19</reference>) to all who call upon Him בּאמת, in firmness, certainty, truth, i.e., so that the prayer comes from their heart and is holy fervour (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.10.20">Isa 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.1">Isa 48:1</reference>). What is meant is true and real prayer in opposition to the νεκρὸν ἔργον, as is also meant in the main in Joh 4:23. To such true praying ones Jahve is present, viz., in mercy (for in respect of His power He is everywhere); He makes the desire of those who fear Him a reality, their will being also His; and He grants them the salvation (σωτηρία) prayed for. Those who are called in <reference osisRef="Ps.145.19">Psa 145:19</reference> those who fear Him, are called in <reference osisRef="Ps.145.20">Psa 145:20</reference> those who love Him. Fear and love of God belong inseparably together; for fear without love is an unfree, servile disposition, and love without fear, bold-faced familiarity: the one dishonours the all-gracious One, and the other the all-exalted One. But all who love and fear Him He preserves, and on the other hand exterminates all wanton sinners. Having reached the <hi type="italic">Tav</hi>, the hymn of praise, which has traversed all the elements of the language, is at an end. The poet does not, however, close without saying that praising God shall be his everlasting employment (פּי ידבּר with <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi>, the <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi> or rather <hi type="italic">Jethib</hi> sign of which above represents the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>), and without wishing that all flesh, i.e., all men, who αρε σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα, בּשׂר ודם, may bless God’s holy Name to all eternity. The realization of this wish is the final goal of history. It will then have reached <reference osisRef="Deut.32.43">Deu 32:43</reference> of the great song in Deut. 32 - - Jahve one and His Name one (Zec 14:9), Israel praising God ὑπὲρ ἀληθείας, and the Gentiles ὑπὲρ ἐλέους (Rom 15:8.).  <chapter eID="Ps.145"/> <div eID="gen10327" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 145
The Psalmist is led to celebrate the praises of God by reflecting upon his excellent wisdom, goodness, and righteousness, both in the government of the world generally, and particularly in managing, superintending, and defending the children of men. After recounting in general the praises of his providence, he comes to speak of the special favor shown by him to his own people.
The Praise of David
This Psalm is with much propriety entitled “Praise of David;” for it is throughout a continued celebration of the perfections and doings of God. It is certainly one of the most interesting and beautiful of the compositions of the sweet singer of Israel; and so high an opinion did the ancient Hebrews form of it that they were wont to say — “Whoever utters this Psalm thrice each day with the heart and tongue is a happy man, and shall infallibly enjoy the blessings of the world to come.” The time and occasion of its composition can only be conjectured. Dr. Morison thinks it probable that it was composed by David when he and the nation of Israel obtained the blessings which he implored in the preceding Psalm; and that it is that new song which he purposed to sing (Psalm 144:9) when God appeared in glory for his chosen people. This is the last of the alphabetical Psalms. The first verse commences with the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, the second verse with the second letter, and so on to the close, with the exception that the hemistich of which נ, nun, was the commencing letter is wanting. The other alphabetical Psalms are Psalm 25, Psalm 34, Psalm 37, Psalm 111, Psalm 112, Psalm 119.
Psalm 145:1-6
1. I will extol thee, my God and my king!
The Jewish government was a theocracy.
and I will bless thy name for ever and ever. 2. Daily I will bless thee, and will praise thy name for ever and ever.
“In seculum et usque.” — Lat. The original Hebrew words are לעילם ועד, leolam vaad, which Dr. Adam Clarke had translated “for ever and onward in this and the coming world.” “These sorts of expressions,” he adds, “are very difficult to be translated.”
3. Great is Jehovah, and greatly to be praised, and there is no searching out, his greatness. 4. Generation to generation, will praise thy works, and will show forth thy power. 5. I will meditate upon
“Ou, parleray.” — Fr. marg. “Or, will speak of.”
the beauty of the glory of thy excellency, and the words of thy wonderful things. 6. And they shall speak of the might of thy terrible works, and I will declare thy greatness.
 
1. I will extol thee, my God and my king. David does not so much tell what he would do himself, as stir up and urge all others to this religious service of offering to God the praises due to his name. The design with which he declares God to be beneficent to the children of men is, to induce them to cultivate a pious gratitude, he insists upon the necessity of persevering in the exercise; for since God is constant in extending mercies, it would be highly improper in us to faint in his praises. As he thus gives his people new ground for praising him, so he stimulates them to gratitude, and to exercise it throughout the whole course of their life. In using the term daily, he denotes perseverance in the exercise. Afterwards he adds, that should he live through a succession of ages he would never cease to act in this manner. The repetitions used tend very considerably to give emphasis to his language. As it is probable that the Psalm was written at a time when the kingdom of David was in a flourishing condition, the circumstances deserves notice, that in calling God his king he gives both himself and other earthly princes their proper place, and does not allow any earthly distinctions to interfere with the glory due to God.
This is made still more manifest in the verse which follows, where, in speaking of the greatness of God as unmeasurable, he intimates that we only praise God aright when we are filled and overwhelmed with an ecstatic admiration of the immensity of his power. This admiration will form the fountain from which our just praises of him will proceed, according the measure of our capacity.

                  <ns0:p n="9">9 The LORD is good to all <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Not to <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> onely, but to all mankind, <ns0:hi>whose hearts he fills with food and gladness,</ns0:hi> as it is said <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 14. 17. yea to all his creatures, as it is in the next clause, to beasts, as well as men. See <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 39. 6. and 147. 9.</ns0:note>: and his tender mercies <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> over all his works.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 All thy works shall praise thee <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Objectively, they give men and Angels just occasion to praise thee.</ns0:note>, O LORD, and thy saints shall bless thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:516" />11 They shall speak of the glory of thy king<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom, and talk of thy power.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 To make known to the sons of men his mighty acts, and the glorious majesty of his king<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Thy kingdom <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> a king<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom of all ages.</ns0:note> an everlasting kingdom, and thy dominion <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> throughout all gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rations.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 The LORD upholdeth all <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either, 1. all that look up to him for help: or, 2. all that are upheld: whose support is not from themselves, nor from other men, but onely from Gods powerful and good providence.</ns0:note> that fall, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 146. 8.</ns0:note> raiseth up all <ns0:hi>those that be</ns0:hi> bowed down.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 The eyes of all <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Of all living creatures.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> look unto thee.</ns0:note> wait upon thee <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Expect and receive their sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plies wholly from thy bounty. Expectation is here figura<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tively ascribed to brute creatures, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 104. 27. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8. 22.</ns0:note>: and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 136. 25.</ns0:note> thou givest them their meat in due season <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">When they need it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 Thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, as divers render it, and which is more agreeable to the order of the words in the Hebrew Text, <ns0:hi>thou satisfiest every living thing</ns0:hi> with thy <ns0:hi>favour</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>good-will, i. e.</ns0:hi> with the fruits of thy bounty: the Pronoun <ns0:hi>thy</ns0:hi> being easily and fitly understood out of the foregoing clause.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 The LORD is righteous in all his ways, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>merciful,</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>bountiful.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> holy <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or rather <ns0:hi>merciful,</ns0:hi> as this word most commonly signifies. There is a mixture of mercy in the most severe and terrible works of God in this life, <ns0:hi>judgment without mercy</ns0:hi> being re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />served for the next life, <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 2. 13. <ns0:hi>Revel.</ns0:hi> 14. 10.</ns0:note> in all his works.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 4. 7.</ns0:note> The LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> nigh unto all them <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">To answer their prayers for relief.</ns0:note> that call upon him, to all that call upon him in truth <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Sincerely or with an upright heart, trusting to him, and waiting upon him in his way.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 He will fulfil the desire <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">So far as it is agreeable to his own will, and convenient for their good; not inordinate desires, which God com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monly denies to his people in mercy, and granteth to his enemies in anger.</ns0:note> of them that fear him: he also will hear their cry, and will save them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 The LORD preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Frequently in this world, but infallibly in the next.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 My mouth shall speak the praise of the LORD: and let all flesh bless his holy Name for ever and ever.</ns0:p>
